abstract:
High-grade serous ovarian cancer (HGSOC) is the deadliest
gynecologic
malignancy in women. The low survival rate is largely due to drug
resistance. Approximately 80% of patients who initially respond to
treatment relapse and become drug-resistant. The lack of effective
second-line therapeutics remains a substantial challenge for BRCA-1/2
wild-type HGSOC patients. Histone Deacetylases (HDACs) are promising
targets in HGSOC treatment; however, the mechanism and efficacy of
HDAC inhibitors are understudied in HGSOC. In order to consider HDACs
as a treatment target, an improved understanding of their function
within HGSOC is required. This includes elucidating HDAC6-specific
protein–protein interactions. In this study, we carried out
substrate trapping followed by liquid chromatography-tandem mass spectrometry
(LC-MS/MS) to elucidate HDAC6 catalytic domain (CD)-specific interactors
in the context of BRCA-1/2 wild-type HGSOC. Overall, this study identified
new HDAC6 substrates that may be unique to HGSOC. The HDAC6-CD1 mutant
condition contained the largest number of significant proteins compared
to the CD2 mutant and the CD1/2 mutant conditions, suggesting the
HDAC6-CD1 domain has catalytic activity that is independent of CD2.
Among the identified substrates were proteins involved in DNA damage
repair including PARP proteins. These findings further justify the
use of HDAC inhibitors as a combination treatment with platinum chemotherapy
agents and PARP inhibitors in HGSOC.

Materials and Methods
HDAC6 Mutant Plasmid Generation and Transfection
HDAC6-mutant
plasmids were generated by Genscript using an HDAC6 OHu63602D plasmid
construct and the pcDNA3.1+/C-(K)-DYK cloning vector using CloneEZ.
Genscript also carried out site-directed mutagenesis of the HDAC6
plasmid construct to obtain plasmids with the following point mutations
in the overall protein structure: H216A, H611A, and H216A/H611A. The
point mutations of the ORF clone of each plasmid were as follows:
H230A, H625A, H230A/H625A.
OVCAR3 cells (ATCC) were cultured
in Roswell Park Memorial Institute (RPMI) 1640 medium supplemented
with 20% fetal bovine serum, 0.01 mg/mL bovine insulin, 1% penicillin/streptomycin,
and 100 μg/mL normocin and maintained at 37 °C with 5%
CO
2
. Cells were seeded at 70% confluency and allowed to
attach for 24 h. The following day, the cells were transfected with
either H216A (CD1), H611A (CD2), H216A/H611A (CD1/2), wild-type HDAC6
(WT) plasmids, or a vehicle control using JetOPTIMUS (Polyplus) in
serum-free, antibiotic-free media. The JetOPTIMUS protocol was optimized
to use 0.5× DNA with a DNA/jetOPTIMUS ratio of 1:1. After 4 h,
the reagent-containing media was replaced with serum-containing media
for 24 h. The cells were then treated with either 10 μM Vorinostat
or DMSO for another 24 h.
Immunoprecipitation
Immunoprecipitation was adapted
from the FLAG Immunoprecipitation Kit protocol for the Anti-FLAG-M2
affinity gel (Millipore Sigma). The transfected cells were washed
twice with ice-cold PBS, and then 500 μL of lysis buffer (50
mM Tris HCl (pH 7.4), 150 mM NaCl, 1 mM EDTA, 1% Triton X-100) was
added to each plate and rocked on ice for 30 min. The lysed cells
were harvested and centrifuged for 10 min at 12,000
g
(4 °C). The supernatant was collected, and the pellet was stored
at −80 °C.
The Anti-FLAG M2 affinity gel suspension
was aliquoted to contain 40 μL of suspension (20 μL of
packed gel volume) per sample. The resin was washed twice in ice-cold
PBS, then 3 times in 1× wash buffer (10× wash buffer: 0.5
M Tris HCl (pH 7.4), 1.5 M NaCl). The resin was centrifuged for 30
s at 5000
g
(4 °C) after each wash. Then, 750
μg of protein was added to each tube containing the washed resin,
and the tube was placed on a rotating rack (end-over end) at 4 °C
overnight.
The resin was centrifuged for 30 s at 5000
g
(4
°C), and the unbound supernatant was carefully removed and stored
at −80 °C. The resin was washed 3 times with 1× wash
buffer and centrifuged for 30 s at 5000
g
(4 °C)
after each wash. Then 30 μL of Bolt 2× LDS sample buffer
(Novex) was added to each sample. Samples were boiled at 95 °C
for 5 min and centrifuged briefly; then, 5 μL of supernatant
was aliquoted from each sample to validate the transfection and immunoprecipitation
via Western blot. The remaining supernatant was stored at −80
°C.
SDS-PAGE and Western Blot
The immunoprecipitation input
and eluted samples were reduced with Bolt 10× sample reducing
agent (Novex) and boiled at 95 °C for 10 min, then loaded on
a Bolt 4–12% Bis-Tris Plus gel (Invitrogen) and run at 200
V for 35 min. The gel was transferred to a nitrocellulose membrane
using semidry transfer for 13 min. After the transfer, the nitrocellulose
membrane was washed 3 times for 5 min with 1× TBS/0.1% Tween-20
(TBS-T), then stained with Ponceau S for 10 min to ensure protein
transfer efficiency. The Ponceau S stain was washed from the membrane
using 1× TBS-T, and then the membrane was blocked in 5% nonfat
milk in 1× TBS-T for 1 h.
The membrane was probed with
a rabbit Monorab DYKDDDDK Tag (Genscript) antibody overnight at 4
°C. The membrane was washed 3 times for 10 min with 1× TBS-T
then incubated with a goat antirabbit IgG-HRP secondary antibody for
1 h at room temperature, then washed 3 min × 10 min with 1×
TBS-T. Chemiluminescence detection was carried out using SuperSignal
West Pico Plus (Thermo Scientific) and CL-Xposure Film (Thermo Scientific)
(
Figure S1
).
SDS-PAGE and In-Gel Digestion
After validating the
efficiency of the transfection and immunoprecipitation, the remaining
25 μL of the sample was loaded on a 4–12% Bis-Tris plus
gel and run at 200 V for 35 min. The gel was stained using Coomassie
blue for 1 h then washed with deionized water for 1 h (
Figure S2
). Each lane/sample was excised into
6 regions. The excised regions were diced into ∼1 mm
3
pieces and placed in 75 μL of 1:1 (Acetonitrile: 100 mM NH
4
HCO
3
), vortexed, and incubated at 4 °C overnight.
The solution was removed and discarded, followed by 2 washes at room
temperature for 15 min. The gel pieces were then dehydrated with 75
μL of 100% acetonitrile for 30 s.
The acetonitrile was
removed, and the gel pieces were rehydrated with 75 μL of 10
mM DTT and incubated for 1 h at 56 °C. After incubating, the
DTT solution was removed, and the gel pieces were washed with 75 μL
of 100 mM NH
4
HCO
3
for 5 min. The NH
4
HCO
3
solution was removed, and 75 μL of 55 mM iodoacetamide
was added to the gel pieces, followed by incubation for 30 min at
room temperature in the dark. The iodoacetamide solution was removed,
and the gel pieces were washed with 75 μL of 1:1 100 mM NH
4
HCO
3
/acetonitrile for 15 min at room temperature.
The solution was removed, and the gel pieces were dehydrated with
100% acetonitrile for 30 s. The gel pieces were rehydrated with 12.5
ng/μL trypsin in 50 mM NH
4
HCO
3
and set
on ice for 15 min. The remaining solution was removed and replaced
with 70 μL of 50 mM NH
4
HCO
3
, and the gel
pieces were incubated at 37 °C overnight.
The supernatant
was recovered in a methanol-rinsed microcentrifuge
tube, and 50 mM NH
4
HCO
3
was added to the gel
pieces for 15 min at room temperature with shaking (400 rpm). The
gel pieces were briefly centrifuged, and the supernatant was added
to the methanol-rinsed tubes. Then, 50% acetonitrile: 5% formic acid
was added to the gel pieces and incubated for 15 min with shaking
(400 rpm) at room temperature. The supernatant was then added to the
supernatant from the previous steps, and this step was repeated twice.
The pooled extracts were then dried in a speed vac and desalted using
C18 STAGE tips.
C18 Stop and Go Extraction (STAGE) Tip Desalting
C18
STAGE tip desalting was carried out based on the method described
by Mertins and Rappsilber.
33
−
35
Briefly, 200 μL C18 STAGE
tips were prepared using two Empore C18 extraction disks. The STAGE
tips were conditioned with 100 μL of acetonitrile and then centrifuged
at 3000
g
for 3 min at room temperature. The STAGE
tips were washed with 100 μL of 50% acetonitrile/0.1% formic
acid. This was followed by equilibration twice with 100 μL of
0.1% formic acid. Samples were loaded onto the conditioned STAGE tips
and washed twice with 100 μL of 0.1% formic acid. Then, the
samples were eluted with 60 μL of 50% acetonitrile/0.1% formic
acid and dried using a speed vac.
Mass Spectrometry Analysis
The peptides were reconstituted
in 5% acetonitrile/0.1% formic acid and analyzed on an Orbitrap Q
Exactive Plus mass spectrometer (Thermo Fisher Scientific) equipped
with an Ultimate 3000 RSLCnano liquid chromatography system. 1/3 of
each sample was injected into an EASY-Spray HPLC Column (75 μm
x 150 mm, 3 μm C18 particle size) with the spray voltage set
to 1.6 kV. Peptides were separated using a 45 min reversed phase gradient
with Solvent A (0.1% formic acid in water) and Solvent B (90% acetonitrile/0.1%
formic acid). The flow rate was set to 0.3 μL/min, and the gradient
was as follows: 0–5 min 3% B, 5–25 min 3–40%
B, 25–26 min 40–90% B, 26-31 min 90% B, 31–32
min 90–3% B, 32–45 min 3% B. Mass spectrometry data
acquisition was carried out using a ddMS
2
IT HCD top 10
method. The full MS scan range was 350–1800
m
/
z
with a resolution of 35,000. Charge states 2+
to 7+ were included with a dynamic exclusion time of 10 s. HCD fragmentation
was carried out using a fixed collision energy of 30% with an isolation
window of 2.0
m
/
z
, resolution of
17,500, AGC target of 1e5, and maximum IT of 50 ms. The raw mass spectrometry
data have been deposited to the ProteomeXchange Consortium
36
via the PRIDE partner repository with the data
set identifier PXD044705.
Mass Spectrometry Data Analysis
Raw mass spectrometry
data was processed using MaxQuant version 2.1.3.0 with the match-between-runs
algorithm and label-free quantification. All other parameters in MaxQuant
were kept under the default settings. A
Homo sapiens
database from Swiss Prot (downloaded August 2022) was modified to
include the sequence of the anti-FLAG M2 antibody (GenBank). This
customized FASTA file was used for protein identification. The protein
groups were then imported into Perseus, and the rows were filtered
by categorical column to remove proteins only identified by site,
reverse sequences, and potential contaminants. The data was then log
2
transformed, and each sample was normalized to the intensity
of the anti-FLAG M2 antibody to account for potential loading differences
across samples, and then median-normalized. Replicates were filtered
individually across samples, and each catalytically inactive mutant
(CD1, CD2, CD1/2) was analyzed individually against its paired wild-type
HDAC6 sample. Proteins that were of higher abundance in the vehicle
control than the wild-type and mutant samples were removed to eliminate
identifications from nonspecific binding. Proteins that had a higher
abundance in the samples treated with Vorinostat were removed to eliminate
potential interactors not present at the catalytic site. Proteins
that were quantified in the mutant sample but not in the wild-type
sample were considered significant. Varying levels of filtering stringency
were applied, similar to the method employed by Nalawansha
et al
.
30
The base filtering (Level
1) required proteins quantified in 2 of the 4 replicates to have log
2
(fold change (FC)) > 0.56 and then to increase the stringency
filtering (Level 2) required proteins quantified in 3 of the 4 replicates
to have log
2
(FC) > 0.56, and a higher stringency (Level
3) required proteins to be quantified in 3 of the 4 replicates to
have log
2
(FC) > 1. Lastly, Level 4 required proteins
to
be quantified across all 4 replicates and a log
2
(FC) >
1 (
Table S1
).
Gene Ontology Analysis
GeneMania in Cytoscape was used
to generate protein-interaction networks. Networks were restricted
to evidence of physical interactions only, and network weighting was
set to equal (by network).
37
Cytoscape
was also used to carry out pathway analysis. Description detail was
automatically set by Cytoscape, and pathways were restricted to experimental
evidence only and significant with a
p
-value of <0.05.
Pie charts were created using GraphPad Prism. The DAVID functional
annotation tool
38
,
39
was used for additional pathway
analysis presented in the bubble plots. Bubble plots were created
using SRplot, a free online platform for data analysis and visualization.

body:
High-grade serous ovarian cancer
(HGSOC) is the deadliest gynecologic malignancy in women
1
with a five-year survival rate of <50%. This
is largely due to late detection, disease relapse, and drug resistance.
2
,
3
Approximately 80% of patients who initially respond to treatment
will relapse and become drug-resistant.
4
The primary standard of care for HGSOC patients includes primary
debulking surgery followed by chemotherapy.
5
There are limited targeted treatments approved for use in HGSOC
including poly(ADP-ribose) polymerase inhibitors (PARPi) (Olaparib,
Niraparib, Rucaparib) and the vascular endothelial growth factor (VEGF)
inhibitor, Bevacizumab.
Bevacizumab was initially approved for
first-line use in combination
with chemotherapy and maintenance therapy.
6
PARPi were initially approved for maintenance therapy in patients
with advanced epithelial ovarian cancer and homologous recombination
(HR) deficient tumors who have had a complete or partial response
to first-line chemotherapy.
7
PARP
proteins bind at sites of single-stranded DNA breaks and recruit
DNA damage repair factors through PARylation signaling. PARPi treatment
of HR-deficient cells is cytotoxic and causes lethal genomic instability
via a phenomenon termed synthetic lethality. PARPi prevent PARP proteins
from repairing single-strand DNA breaks, which results in the formation
of double-strand DNA breaks. Two major pathways exist for the repair
of double-strand DNA breaks: HR and nonhomologous end joining (NHEJ).
HR is a high-fidelity DNA damage repair pathway that occurs in the
G2/S phase of the cell cycle. HR-deficient cells utilize NHEJ, which
typically occurs in the G1 phase and occurs at a faster rate than
HR. However, NHEJ is error-prone.
8
−
11
Although PARPi are approved
for use as a monotherapy, the development
of PARPi resistance remains a significant challenge for HGOSC patients.
This has led to the development of PARPi combination therapies. HR
status has been used to stratify patients for treatment with PARPi
and immune checkpoint inhibitors. Evidence that HR deficiency can
result in a higher neoantigen load, likely due to HR defects, has
led to the assessment of the combination of PARPi with immune checkpoint
inhibitors; however, this treatment approach is in the preclinical
testing phase.
12
The FDA-approved
intended uses for Bevacizumab and Olaparib have
been extended to include their use in combination with each other
as a first-line therapy.
6
However, the
use of these targeted inhibitors only extends progression-free survival
by an average of 6–18 months.
6
,
13
When disease
recurrence occurs, there is a lack of alternative treatments to pursue,
and this absence of alternative therapeutic options remains a significant
challenge, especially in the setting of HR proficiency. This led to
the investigation of alternative drug targets, including histone deacetylases
(HDACs).
HDACs are a group of enzymes that modulate gene expression
through
the removal of acetyl functional groups from lysine amino acid residues
on histone and nonhistone proteins. There are 18 different HDACs that
are divided into four classes: I, II, III, and IV. The different classes
are distinguished by localization and sequence homology.
14
,
15
HDAC6, a class IIb HDAC, is the largest member of the HDAC family
based on the number of amino acids. HDAC6 has a significant role in
many cellular processes and, specifically, in cancer-related pathways.
These pathways and processes include cell motility, stress response,
autophagy, apoptosis, proliferation, and migration.
16
−
20
Previous studies have associated increased HDAC6
expression levels with poor prognosis and chemotherapy resistance
in HGSOC,
15
,
18
making HDAC6 a promising target for cancer
treatment.
HDAC6 is a primarily cytoplasmic enzyme
15
,
21
that contains an internal duplication of two catalytic domains (CD).
The two domains are believed to have separate substrate targets.
22
−
24
Previous studies have shown that the CD1 and CD2 domains both contain
deacetylase activity,
25
,
26
while others have claimed that
only CD2 is catalytically active.
27
The
contradictory functionality between CD1 and CD2 domains may be due
to differing methods of analysis, such as the use of recombinant purified
proteins versus cell lysates or the variable utility of the opposing
domains across cell types. Nevertheless, the exact functional roles
of CD1 and CD2 are not well-established.
The function of HDACs
and their role in cancer progression and
development have led to the development and implementation of HDAC
inhibitors (HDACi). However, HDACi has yet to gain FDA approval for
intended uses related to HGSOC treatment. There is still much unknown
regarding the role of HDACi and, specifically, their function in HGSOC.
29
In order to consider HDACs as a therapeutic
target in HGSOC we
need to better understand their function in HGSOC, including their
protein–protein interactions. Applying a catalytically inactive
mutant allows substrates to bind to enzymes for a longer period of
time and enables the detection of interacting proteins, including
transient interactors, using immunoprecipitation coupled with mass
spectrometry analysis, as described previously.
28
−
31
Mass spectrometry-basedanalysis
can facilitate a comprehensive understanding of the HGSOC proteome,
thereby enabling the elucidation of functional consequences of genomic
changes.
32
This analytical approach can
also enable the identification of new therapeutic vulnerabilities
to decrease drug resistance.
In this study, we carried out the
method of substrate trapping
to identify novel HDAC6 interactors in the context of HR-proficient
HGSOC using catalytically inactive mutants of HDAC6 having mutations
in either CD1 (H216A), CD2 (H611A), or CD1 and CD2 (CD1/2) (H216A/H611A).
We found that the CD1 and CD2 domains had unique substrates, suggesting
that both domains are catalytically active. HDAC6 interactions also
overlapped between the two domains. DNA damage repair factors and
PARP proteins were among the HDAC6-interacting proteins identified
using both of the catalytically inactive mutants, which provides justification
for combination treatments of HDAC inhibitors with PARP inhibitors
in HGSOC.

Results and Discussion
Substrate Trapping Overview
In this study, we utilized
the method of substrate trapping to identify catalytic domain-specific
substrates of HDAC6 in the context of HGSOC. Substrate trapping is
an effective method that enables the characterization of transiently
bound substrates of an enzyme of interest. This method is carried
out by transfecting a catalytically inactive mutant of an enzyme into
cells. The inactive enzyme then binds its substrates for an extended
period of time, allowing for immunoprecipitation of the enzyme with
its bound substrates. This is then followed by protein digestion and
mass spectrometry analysis, which enables robust identification and
quantification of potential substrates.
We used three catalytically
inactive HDAC6 mutants in this study: one containing a point mutation
in catalytic domain 1 (CD1) (H216A), the second containing a point
mutation in CD2 (H611A), and the third containing a dual point mutation
in CD1 & CD2 (H216A/H611A) (
Figure
1
A). These point mutations have been used in previous
studies of HDAC6 catalytic activity.
31
,
42
When filtering
the data, we used four levels of stringency (
Table S1
,
Figure
1
B). The base level of stringency (L1) required 2 of the 4 replicates
to have a log
2
(FC) > 0.56. This level of filtering was
used for pathway and network analyses.

However, the CD1 and CD2 mutants resulted in the identification of

The interaction of HDAC6 with multiple PTM regulators could be
beneficial in determining the downstream impacts of inhibiting HDAC
activity. The abundant HDAC6-kinase interactions could support a functional
justification for the development of HDACi and kinase inhibitor combination
therapies. This information could also be utilized to guide the development
of alternative therapeutic opportunities for HGSOC.
Conclusions
In this study, we carried out substrate
trapping to analyze HDAC6
interactors in the context of HGSOC. To consider HDACs as therapeutic
targets, there is a need for an enhanced understanding of their function
in HGSOC, including identifying their interacting proteins. The identification
of HDAC targets will enable us to define their biological roles with
functional consequences related to disease aggressiveness and drug
sensitivity in HGSOC. The identification of HDAC substrates can lead
to the development of more targeted therapeutics to minimize off-target
effects from HDACi.
We hypothesized that HDAC6 interacts with
proteins involved in
DNA damage repair and transcription to promote tumor progression and
drug resistance. This analysis was carried out using three different
catalytically dead HDAC6 mutants to determine the catalytic domain-specific
HDAC6 interactors.
Our identification of HDAC6 interactions
with multiple PARP proteins
further justifies the utility of HDAC inhibitors in combination with
PARP inhibitors. However, the best combination of which PARP inhibitor
and HDAC inhibitor to utilize together has yet to be determined. Two
clinical trials evaluated the utility of HDAC inhibitors in combination
with PARP inhibitors. Phase I clinical trial
NCT03924245
assessed
the utility of HDACi Entinostat with PARPi Olaparib in platinum-resistant
ovarian cancers. The study was terminated in 2022 due to a lack of
results and publication. A Phase I clinical trial assessing PARPi
Talazoparib and HDACi Belinostat in metastatic ovarian cancer is currently
recruiting participants (
NCT04703920
).
One limitation of our
study is the endogenous HDAC6 expression
within the OVCAR3 cells, given that a knockdown or knockout biochemical
approach was not pursued. Future work could incorporate the use of
HDAC6 knockout cells. Our next steps include additional validation
of the HDAC6 substrates identified in this study, expansion of this
method into additional HGSOC cell lines with differing genetic backgrounds,
and different types of ovarian cancer cell lines (non-high-grade serous).
Supplementary studies can also be carried out to distinguish the hierarchy
of the identified interacting proteins and whether these proteins
are direct interactors or the result of protein complex formation.
Future studies could incorporate the investigation of the non-catalytic
domains of HDAC6, such as the ubiquitin-binding domain, to assess
additional HDAC6-interacting proteins that are independent of its
catalytic activity.
Overall, this study identified new HDAC6
substrates that may be
unique to ovarian cancer models. Additional substrates were also implicated
in DNA damage repair, which further justifies the use of HDACi as
a combination treatment with platinum chemotherapy agents and/or targeted
inhibitors, such as PARP inhibitors, in ovarian cancer. Further investigation
of other previously unknown substrates could elucidate their roles
in HGSOC and their potential therapeutic utility. The identification
of HDAC6 substrates and the role of these interactions could lead
to the development of inhibitors targeting specific proteins that
may be unique to ovarian cancer, expand treatment options, and improve
overall patient survival.
